title: Recognizing KServe and Kubeflow
intro: Many production ML platforms add their own custom resources on top of Kubernetes. You don't need to be a Kubeflow expert, but you do need to find your way around one — and it's all just kubectl and CRDs underneath.

steps.prompt: List the KServe InferenceServices (model deployments) in the current namespace.
steps.fake_output:
NAME          URL                                     READY  PREV  LATEST
fraud-model   http://fraud-model.ml.example.com       True   90    10
steps.explanation: One model, with 90% of traffic on the previous revision and 10% on the latest — a canary in progress.
steps.why: An InferenceService is a custom resource (see tutorial-018 on CRDs) that KServe's operator turns into deployments, autoscaling, and routing. Same get/describe verbs as any built-in resource.

steps.prompt: Get the full details of the fraud-model InferenceService.
steps.fake_output:
Spec:
  Predictor:
    Model:
      Model Format: sklearn
      Storage Uri:  s3://models/fraud/v7
    Canary Traffic Percent: 10
Status:
  Conditions:
    Type: Ready  Status: True
steps.explanation: The model artifact lives in S3; KServe pulls and serves it.
steps.why: The Storage Uri is what to check first when a new model version misbehaves — it tells you exactly which artifact is live.

steps.prompt: Check that the Kubeflow platform components are healthy.
steps.fake_output:
NAME                                   READY  STATUS
ml-pipeline-7d8f9c6b5-x2z9k            1/1    Running
ml-pipeline-ui-6b8d9f7c4-a1b2c          1/1    Running
metadata-grpc-deployment-5f6d7c8b9      0/1    CrashLoopBackOff
steps.explanation: The metadata service is crash-looping — pipeline runs will fail to record lineage.
steps.why: Kubeflow is a collection of ordinary Kubernetes workloads. When 'Kubeflow is broken', debugging it uses exactly the skills from the Kubernetes category: get pods, logs, describe.

steps.explanation: The pipeline's steps (fetch data, train, evaluate, register) run as pods.
steps.why: Pipelines make training repeatable and auditable in the same way CI makes builds repeatable — the training run is defined as code, not as a sequence of notebook cells someone ran once.
